name: AVCD

question.stem: A male infant with Trisomy 21 is undergoing routine screening echocardiography in the NICU, as recommended for all infants with Down syndrome regardless of clinical exam findings. The echocardiogram reveals a complete atrioventricular (AV) canal defect with a common AV valve, a large primum atrial septal defect, and a large inlet ventricular septal defect. An EKG shows severe left axis deviation ("superior QRS axis") and biventricular hypertrophy.
question.prompt: If this lesion is left uncorrected, this patient is at greatest risk for developing which of the following?

options.text: Irreversible pulmonary vascular obstructive disease (Eisenmenger syndrome)

explanation.text: Complete AV canal defect creates a large, unrestricted communication at both the atrial and ventricular levels, combined with a common AV valve that is often regurgitant. This results in massive left-to-right shunting and marked pulmonary overcirculation, exposing the pulmonary vasculature to both high flow and, given the ventricular-level communication, near-systemic pressure from birth.

Infants with Trisomy 21 are uniquely predisposed to develop pulmonary vascular obstructive disease at an accelerated pace and younger age compared to euploid infants with the same lesion. Proposed mechanisms include intrinsically abnormal pulmonary vascular development (fewer alveoli, thicker medial smooth muscle in pulmonary arterioles), a higher incidence of upper airway obstruction/obstructive sleep apnea, and a higher incidence of chronic hypoventilation — all of which compound pulmonary hypertensive changes. Left uncorrected, this progresses to irreversible pulmonary vascular remodeling, elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, and eventual shunt reversal (Eisenmenger physiology), at which point the defect becomes inoperable.

This is precisely why complete AV canal repair is recommended early, typically by 3–6 months of age, in Down syndrome patients — earlier than might otherwise be pursued in a euploid infant with the same anatomy — specifically to prevent this irreversible complication.

content.text: Left heart failure: While pulmonary overcirculation does cause volume loading and can contribute to symptoms of heart failure (poor feeding, diaphoresis, poor weight gain) prior to surgical repair, this is a treatable, reversible physiologic consequence of the shunt — it is not the defining long-term consequence of an uncorrected lesion the way irreversible pulmonary vascular disease is.

Right heart failure: Similarly can occur as a downstream consequence of chronic pulmonary hypertension, but it develops as a result of the pulmonary vascular changes described in answer C, rather than being the primary long-term threat itself.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Not a recognized complication of unrepaired AV canal defect.

Complete heart block: AV canal defects are associated with an abnormally positioned AV node (displaced due to the malaligned septal structures) and increased postoperative risk of heart block, but this is a surgical/iatrogenic risk, not a natural consequence of leaving the lesion uncorrected.

bottomLine: Complete AV canal defect causes large-volume, high-pressure left-to-right shunting, and Trisomy 21 patients are at particularly high risk for early, accelerated, irreversible pulmonary vascular obstructive disease (Eisenmenger syndrome) if the defect is not surgically corrected — driving the recommendation for early repair (by 3–6 months) in this population.
